opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a fair amount. When I graduated in 2016, the path that made sense for someone like me, who liked thinking carefully about big, fuzzy questions and wanted to help the world, was to join Open Philanthropy, then GiveWell Labs, and do this sort of generalist research: reading a lot, building spreadsheet models, trying to reason about which causes mattered most. That kind of work was what I was drawn to, and it led me into AI forecasting with the biological anchors report.

If I were graduating in 2022, I think the preference for research would still be there, but I'd feel a lot more pressure to point it at something more empirical and hands-on. By 2022 you could already see that large language models were going to be a big deal, and a lot of the most important open questions about AI had shifted. They were less about "when might this happen, in principle," which you could attack with armchair modeling, and more about "what are these systems actually doing, how do we evaluate them, how do we know if they're dangerous." Those questions are best answered by people who can run experiments on real models.

So I suspect I'd have tried harder to build technical skills, learn ML properly, and get into an empirical alignment or evaluations role, maybe at a lab or one of the safety-focused nonprofits doing evals and interpretability. Honestly, I sometimes wish I'd done more of that even on my actual timeline. I think there's still a place for the conceptual, big-picture synthesis work I've done. Someone has to step back and ask what all the empirical results add up to. But the marginal value has shifted toward people who can get their hands dirty with the systems themselves.

The other thing is that in 2022 it was much less clear that the slow, reflective, multi-year research project was the right format. Things move so fast now that a report that takes two years to write can be out of date by the time it's published. So I'd probably also have leaned toward shorter feedback loops: smaller pieces, faster iteration, more direct engagement with what's happening in the field week to week.

r001.rationale: She says she would have pursued empirical alignment or evaluations research at an AI lab or safety-focused nonprofit, linking that choice to her continuing preference for research.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention diminished leadership-level demand for research at Open Philanthropy as a reason to avoid joining it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a funny question to think about, because when I graduated in 2016 the landscape was really different. I came out of Berkeley having done EA stuff as a student, and the thing I wanted was to work on questions that felt important and under-explored, and at the time that meant something like Open Phil, where I could do very generalist research — trying to think about how big a deal AI would be, what timelines looked like, how much money should go where. There weren't that many places doing that kind of work, and honestly the bar for being useful was lower, because so few people were paying attention.

If I were graduating in 2022, I think I'd feel a lot more pull toward the technical side. Not necessarily because I think conceptual or forecasting work is less important — I still think it matters a lot — but because the field has moved. In 2022 the models were already good enough that you could run real experiments on the questions I used to only be able to reason about from the armchair. Things like, does a model generalize in the way we'd want when you train it a certain way, can you detect when it's being deceptive, how does behavior scale. A lot of what I did in the bio anchors report was essentially trying to triangulate from indirect evidence, and now you can just go look, at least for some of these questions.

So I think I'd probably try to get an ML background, maybe go do a master's or just skill up on my own, and aim to work on alignment or evals at a lab or at a place like ARC or Redwood. The empirical work seems like where the marginal person can contribute the most right now, and it's also where my own curiosity would pull me — I like having a tight feedback loop with reality, and forecasting doesn't give you that very often.

That said, I'd want to caveat it. The thing I actually enjoy, and I think am reasonably good at, is sitting with a big messy question and trying to make it a little more tractable — decomposing it, figuring out what the cruxes are. That's a skill that transfers to empirical research, but it's not the same as being a strong engineer, and I think a 2022 version of me would have to be honest about whether I'd be good at that. There's also a bit of a crowding effect: a lot of smart people are now flowing into technical alignment, and there's still a real shortage of people who can do the strategy and governance thinking well, who can talk to policymakers, who can figure out what the actual decision-relevant questions are. So I don't think the answer is just "everyone should go do ML." It's more that if you have the aptitude for it, the opportunity cost of not trying is higher than it was in 2016, and I'd want to at least test that in myself before defaulting to the generalist path.

r001.rationale: She says she would likely build an ML background and aim for alignment or evaluation work at a lab or AI safety research organization, showing that research preference would pull her toward that field in 2022.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention reduced demand for leadership-level research at Open Philanthropy as a reason to avoid joining it.

astra-6.text:
I think I’d be pretty torn. I really like doing research myself, and I think that would pull me toward trying to work directly on AI alignment. If I were graduating in 2022, I’d want to spend some time actually trying that work and seeing whether I could contribute, rather than assuming that enjoying research in general meant I’d be good at that particular kind of research.

But I’d also want to distinguish what I find most interesting from where I could be most useful. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing. So my preference for research would definitely shape what I tried first, but I wouldn’t want it to settle the career decision on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says her research preference would pull her toward trying AI alignment work, but it does not say she would join an AI safety research group.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Open Philanthropy or diminished leadership-level demand for research there.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’d still be pretty drawn to research, but I’d want to test that preference against actually doing the work. There’s a difference between enjoying thinking about big questions and enjoying the day-to-day process of making progress on a question where you’re confused for a long time.

If I were graduating in 2022, I’d probably be looking pretty seriously at opportunities to work on AI alignment or on research that helps us understand how AI is going to develop. I’d want to find a concrete project, work with people I could learn from, and see whether I was useful at it. I wouldn’t necessarily assume that meant going straight into a PhD. I think the important thing would be getting a feedback loop: do I like this work, am I getting better at it, and does it seem like it could matter?

r001.rationale: She says she would seriously consider opportunities to work on AI alignment research, find a concrete project, and work with people she could learn from.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Open Philanthropy or diminished leadership-level demand for research there.
